s1_definition.profdef: The Shared Responsibility Model is the cloud security contract that divides duties between the provider and the customer. The provider is responsible for security "of" the cloud — the physical data centers, hardware, hypervisor, and the managed-service control plane. The customer is responsible for security "in" the cloud — their data, identity and access configuration, network rules, encryption settings, operating-system patching, and application code. Most breaches happen on the customer side because the provider's half is hardened by thousands of engineers, while the customer's half depends on correct configuration that is easy to get wrong.

The bank secures the vault door, the walls, the guards, and the alarm system — that is their responsibility. If National Bank of India leaves a box wide open and money is stolen, that is not the vault builder's fault — it is the account holder's. s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Shared Responsibility Model is the cloud security contract that divides duties between the provider and the customer. The provider is responsible for security "of" the cloud — the physical data centers, hardware, hypervisor, and the managed-service control plane. The customer is responsible for security "in" the cloud — their data, identity and access configuration, network rules, encryption settings, operating-system patching, and application code. Most breaches happen on the customer side because the provider's half is hardened by thousands of engineers, while the customer's half depends on correct configuration that is easy to get wrong.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The cloud provider is the bank building that rents you a safe-deposit box. The bank secures the vault door, the walls, the guards, and the alarm system — that is their responsibility. But you are given the key to your own box, and you decide whether to lock it, who you hand copies of the key to, and whether you leave the box open on the counter. If National Bank of India leaves a box wide open and money is stolen, that is not the vault builder's fault — it is the account holder's. In the cloud, a public storage bucket or an over-powerful access key is the box left open on the counter.

**One line to remember:** The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it — and nearly every breach is someone leaving their own box unlocked.

sections.s2_technical:
The exact dividing line moves depending on which service model you use, and this is the part engineers most often get wrong. With Infrastructure-as-a-Service, such as raw virtual machines, the provider secures the hardware and hypervisor but you own everything from the guest operating system upward — that means you patch the OS, configure the firewall, manage identities, and encrypt your data. With Platform-as-a-Service and managed services like a managed database or object storage, the provider also takes over the OS and runtime patching, so your responsibility shrinks to data, access policies, and configuration. With Software-as-a-Service the provider runs almost everything and your responsibility narrows mostly to managing who has access and how your data is classified. The senior-level insight is that your responsibility never drops to zero — in every model you always own your data and your identity-and-access configuration.

Now, why do the breaches cluster on the customer side? The provider's half is operated at enormous scale by dedicated security teams, independently audited, and standardized, so a flaw there is rare and quickly fixed for everyone. The customer's half, by contrast, is bespoke: every company wires up its own buckets, roles, security groups, and encryption settings, and any one of thousands of small choices can open a hole. Industry analysts have repeatedly projected that the overwhelming majority of cloud security failures through this decade stem from customer misconfiguration rather than provider failure.

The two most common customer-side failures are misconfiguration and over-permissioned identities. Misconfiguration means a setting that silently exposes data: an object-storage bucket made public, a database with a public endpoint and a default password, logging turned off so you cannot even see an attack, or encryption left disabled. Over-permissioned identities means an access key, role, or user that has far more power than it needs — the classic anti-pattern is attaching a wildcard policy that grants all actions on all resources to a service that only ever needs to read one bucket. When that over-powerful credential leaks, through a committed secret or a compromised laptop, the blast radius is the entire account rather than one bucket.

The defenses are the inverse of these failures. Against misconfiguration you use infrastructure-as-code so settings are reviewed and version-controlled rather than clicked in a console, plus automated posture scanning that continuously checks for public buckets and open ports. Against over-permissioning you apply least privilege — grant only the specific actions on the specific resources a workload needs — and you prefer short-lived temporary credentials from role assumption over long-lived static keys. You enforce encryption at rest and in transit by default, you turn on audit logging everywhere, and you use guardrail policies that make it impossible to, for example, create a public bucket in the first place. The whole philosophy is to make the secure configuration the only configuration that is allowed.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the platform team is auditing a new account-statements service that stores PDF statements in cloud object storage and runs on managed compute. They want a tool that classifies each cloud control as the provider's responsibility or the bank's, and then flags the bank-side controls that are misconfigured — because those are the ones that actually cause breaches.

Problem 1 — The statements storage bucket has been set to public read so that a quick internal demo could link to a PDF, and nobody turned it back. This is exactly how a misconfiguration breach happens — the data is exposed not because the provider failed but because a customer-side access setting was left open. The tool must flag this as a customer responsibility that is in a failing state.

Problem 2 — The service's access role was given a wildcard "all actions on all resources" policy because it was faster than figuring out the exact permissions. This is exactly how an over-permissioned identity happens — if that role's credentials leak, the attacker owns the whole account. The tool must flag this as a critical customer-side failure.

Problem 3 — The underlying physical data center security and the hypervisor patching are handled by the provider. This is exactly how the "security of the cloud" half works — the tool must classify these as provider responsibilities that the bank does not need to audit.

Problem 4 — Encryption at rest on the bucket is enabled and audit logging is turned on. This is exactly how a correctly configured customer-side control looks — the tool classifies them as the bank's responsibility and marks them compliant.

The code will model a `CloudControl` with a responsible party and a compliance state, a `ResponsibilityClassifier` that separates provider controls from customer controls, and a `BreachRiskAuditor` that reports only the customer-side controls that are failing, since those are the real breach surface. We will run the four controls above and show which ones the bank must fix.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
cloud-responsibility-auditor/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/cloud/
│   │   │   ├── CloudAuditApplication.java          (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   ├── ResponsibleParty.java            (enum)
│   │   │   │   ├── ComplianceState.java             (enum)
│   │   │   │   └── CloudControl.java
│   │   │   ├── classify/
│   │   │   │   └── ResponsibilityClassifier.java
│   │   │   └── audit/
│   │   │       └── BreachRiskAuditor.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── responsibility-matrix.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/cloud/
│           └── audit/
│               └── BreachRiskAuditorTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# responsibility-matrix.yml — who owns what, by service model
model: managed-service   # PaaS-style: provider patches OS, bank owns data+access
provider-owns:
  - physical-datacenter
  - hypervisor-patching
  - managed-control-plane
customer-owns:
  - bucket-access-policy
  - iam-role-permissions
  - encryption-at-rest
  - audit-logging
guardrails:
  deny-public-buckets: true      # make the insecure state impossible
  require-encryption: true
  max-policy-scope: least-privilege
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four controls — a public statements bucket owned by the bank and misconfigured, a wildcard role owned by the bank and misconfigured, the physical data center plus hypervisor owned by the provider and compliant, and encryption-plus-logging owned by the bank and compliant.

Step 1: The application builds the four controls and passes them as one list to the classifier. Each control still carries its party and compliance state unchanged.

Step 2: The classifier filters by responsible party equal to provider. Only the data center control matches, so it logs that the provider secures one control that the bank need not audit. The data itself is unchanged; the classifier only reads it.

Step 3: The classifier filters by responsible party equal to customer. Three controls match — the bucket, the role, and the encryption control — and it logs that the bank is accountable for three controls.

Step 4: The auditor receives only the three customer-owned controls and filters them by the breach-risk test, which is true only when a control is customer-owned and misconfigured. The bucket passes the test because it is public, the role passes because it is a wildcard policy, and the encryption control fails the test because it is compliant.

Step 5: The auditor finds two breach risks. It logs a SEVERE message for the public bucket and another for the wildcard role, including the human-readable detail for each so the engineer knows exactly what to fix.

Step 6: The application prints that the bank must remediate two controls to close the breach surface. The provider-owned control never appears in the risk list, which reinforces the core lesson: the breaches live on the customer side.

Final output:

```
INFO: === National Bank of India — Shared Responsibility audit ===
INFO: Provider secures 1 control(s) — bank need not audit these
INFO: Bank is accountable for 3 control(s)
SEVERE: BREACH RISK (customer-owned): statements-bucket-access — bucket set to PUBLIC read — statements exposed to the internet
SEVERE: BREACH RISK (customer-owned): service-iam-role — role grants all-actions-on-all-resources — blast radius = whole account
INFO: Bank must remediate 2 control(s) to close breach surface
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Shared Responsibility Model is the security contract that splits duties between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud — the physical data centers, the hardware, the hypervisor, and the managed-service control plane — while the customer is responsible for security in the cloud, which means their data, their identity and access configuration, their network rules, their encryption settings, and their application code. The crucial detail is that the dividing line moves depending on the service model: with raw virtual machines I own everything from the guest operating system up, with managed services the provider takes over the OS and runtime so my responsibility shrinks to data and access, and with software-as-a-service I mostly just manage who has access. But my responsibility never reaches zero — in every model I always own my data and my identity configuration.

The reason almost every cloud breach lands on the customer side is structural. The provider's half is run at massive scale by dedicated security teams, independently audited and standardized, so flaws there are rare and fixed for everyone at once. The customer's half is bespoke — every company wires up its own buckets, roles, and firewall rules, and any one of thousands of small configuration choices can open a hole. Industry analysts have consistently projected that the overwhelming majority of cloud security failures this decade come from customer misconfiguration, not provider failure.

The two failures that dominate are misconfiguration and over-permissioned identities. Misconfiguration is a setting that silently exposes data — a storage bucket made public, a database with a public endpoint and a default password, or logging switched off so you cannot even see the attack. Over-permissioning is a credential that has far more power than it needs, like a role granted all actions on all resources when it only needs to read one bucket, so when that credential leaks the blast radius is the whole account instead of one object.

The defenses are the mirror image of those failures, and this is exactly what I implemented at National Bank of India. I put all configuration into infrastructure-as-code so settings are reviewed and version-controlled instead of clicked in a console, I run continuous posture scanning to catch public buckets and open ports, I enforce least privilege with short-lived temporary credentials instead of long-lived static keys, and I turn on encryption and audit logging by default. I even built an auditor that classifies every control as provider-owned or bank-owned and then reports only the bank-owned misconfigurations, because those are the real breach surface — and the philosophy behind all of it is to use guardrails so that the secure configuration is the only configuration anyone is even allowed to create.
